field1: A Cessna 172 on its takeoff roll is at 10 knots 4 seconds after brake release and at 40 knots 14 seconds after brake release. What is its average acceleration?
field2:
3 knots per second

(40 kt − 10 kt) ÷ (14 s − 4 s) = 30 kt ÷ 10 s
field3: Every second of the roll, the airplane gains 3 knots.

field1: A car is moving forward but slowing down. Which way does its acceleration point?
field2:
Opposite to its velocity, toward the rear. When the car speeds up, acceleration points the same way as velocity.

Example: braking after touchdown. The airplane still rolls forward, but its acceleration points backward.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides

field1: A gas is trapped in a cylinder. At constant temperature, what happens to its pressure when the piston pushes in and reduces the volume?
field2:
Pressure increases (high pressure ↔ low volume; low pressure ↔ high volume).

The compression stroke uses this idea: the piston shrinks the space, so the pressure rises. There the temperature rises too, which pushes the pressure even higher.
field3: This is Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant temperature.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides

field1: Forms of energy at work in an aircraft: {{c1::heat (thermal)}}, {{c2::mechanical}}, {{c3::electrical}}, {{c4::chemical}}.
field2:
In the engine, energy changes form in a chain: chemical (fuel) → heat (combustion) → mechanical (crankshaft and propeller) → electrical (alternator).
Other forms of energy exist too, such as nuclear, radiant (light) and sound.

field1: Math: a hoist lifts a 550-lb load 20 feet in 20 seconds. How much horsepower does it produce?
field2:
1 horsepower

Work = 550 lb × 20 ft = 11,000 ft-lb
Power = 11,000 ft-lb ÷ 20 s = 550 ft-lb per second
550 ft-lb per second = 1 hp
field3: Do the same lift in 10 seconds and it takes 2 hp: same work, half the time, twice the power.

field1: Math: a tug pushes an airplane with a steady force of 300 lb and moves it 50 feet. How much work does it do?
field2:
15,000 ft-lb

Work = force × distance
300 lb × 50 ft = 15,000 ft-lb
field3: If the airplane didn't move, the work would be zero, however hard the tug pushed.

field1: Math: burning gas pushes on a 20-square-inch piston with a force of 10,000 lb. What is the pressure in the cylinder?
field2:
500 psi

Pressure = force ÷ area
10,000 lb ÷ 20 sq in = 500 psi
field3: Turned around: force = pressure × area. psi means pounds per square inch, so 500 lb on each of 20 square inches adds up to 10,000 lb.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W1_P51 Matter ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1225 Updated1005 Week1
field1: Melting, vaporization and ionization (solid → liquid → gas → plasma): what happens to energy in these changes?
field2:
Energy is added (heat goes in). The molecules need more energy to move faster and spread farther apart.

Example: fuel takes in heat as it vaporizes in the carburetor. That cools the air, which is one cause of carburetor ice.
field3: The reverse changes (freezing, condensation, deionization) remove energy.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W1_P09 Matter ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1220 Updated1005 Week1
field1:
Phase changes:
solid → liquid = {{c1::melting}}
liquid → solid = {{c2::freezing}}
liquid → gas = {{c3::vaporization}}
gas → liquid = {{c4::condensation}}
gas → plasma = {{c5::ionization}}
plasma → gas = {{c6::deionization}}
field2: Aviation example: fuel has to vaporize (liquid → gas) before it can burn, which is why the carburetor or fuel injector breaks it into a fine spray.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides

field1: Physical property of matter: what is density?
field2:
The mass of an object compared to its volume.

Example: hot air is less dense than cold air, so the engine takes in less air per stroke and makes less power on a hot day.
field3: Density = mass ÷ volume.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W1_P14 Matter ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1280 Updated1005 Week1
field1: Physical property of matter: what is inertia?
field2:
The characteristic of matter that resists a change in motion (in velocity or direction).

Example: in turbulence your body keeps moving while the airplane changes direction, which is why you wear a seat belt.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W1_P15 Matter ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1290 Updated1005 Week1
field1: Physical property of matter: what is mass?
field2:
A measure of a body's inertia, and a measure of the quantity of matter in the body.

Mass stays the same anywhere; weight changes with gravity. An engine on the Moon has the same mass but weighs about one-sixth as much.
field3: The vocabulary handout puts it simply: "the amount of matter in an object."

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W1_P13 Matter ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1260 Updated1005 Week1
field1: Physical property of matter: what is volume?
field2:
The amount of space an object occupies, measured in cubic units (length × width × height, e.g., cubic inches) or in liters.

Example: the Archer's O-360 gets its name from volume: its pistons sweep 360 cubic inches in all.
field3: Length and width alone measure area; volume needs all three dimensions.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W1_P16 Matter ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1300 Updated1005 Week1
field1: Physical property of matter: what is weight?
field2:
The gravitational force of attraction between the Earth and a body (mass) near the Earth.

Weight = mass × gravity. Weight, not mass, is what the wings have to lift.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 FrictionEnergy ID_W1_P32 ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1450 Updated1005 Week1
field1:
Types of friction:
{{c1::Static}} friction acts between surfaces that are at rest relative to each other.
{{c2::Sliding}} friction is the resistance between two objects sliding against each other.
{{c3::Rolling}} friction resists the motion of a ball or wheel.
field2: Aircraft examples: static = the parking brake holding the airplane on a sloped ramp; sliding = a skidding tire; rolling = the tires on the takeoff roll. Static friction is usually stronger than sliding friction, which is why it takes more push to start a towed airplane moving than to keep it moving.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides

Example: one trip around the traffic pattern covers several miles of distance, even though you end up back where you started.

field1: What is force?
field2:
A push or pull on an object that can cause it to change its velocity.

Examples: thrust, drag, lift and weight on the airplane; gas pressure pushing on the piston inside the engine.
field3: The vocabulary handout says the same thing: "a push or pull that can change an object's motion."

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 FrictionEnergy ID_W1_P31 ProfSlides Quiz1 Seq_1440 Updated1005 Week1
field1: What is friction?
field2:
A contact force that opposes the relative motion, or attempted motion, between two surfaces or through fluids.

Example: friction between the piston rings and the cylinder wall turns some engine power into heat and wear. Oil cuts it down.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 01 · Quiz 1 · Physics — Professor Slides

field1: What is kinematics?
field2:
The study of objects in motion: the relationship between velocity, acceleration, and distance.

It describes how something moves (how fast, how far, how quickly the speed changes, how long it takes) without asking what causes the motion.
field3: Dynamics adds the forces: it asks why the motion happens. On the takeoff roll, kinematics asks how fast and how far; dynamics asks why the airplane speeds up (thrust is bigger than drag plus wheel friction).

field1: What is the difference between inertia and momentum?

Inertia is a property of matter: its resistance to any change in motion. It depends only on mass and exists even at rest.
Momentum is mass × velocity. It depends on both mass and speed, and it is zero when the body is at rest.

field1: What is the study of dynamics?
field2:
The study of the relationship between the motion of bodies and the forces acting on them. It is also called force and motion.

It explains why something moves the way it does: forces cause every change in motion.
field3: Kinematics is the narrower study of velocity, acceleration, and distance: it describes how something moves without the forces. Example: on the takeoff roll the airplane speeds up because thrust is bigger than drag plus wheel friction.

field1: Why are railroad couplings built with a few inches of slack?

field1: Why are sinusoidal waveforms common in matter?

field1: Power stroke: what happens?
field2:
The spark plug ignites the compressed mixture, and the expanding gases force the piston away from the cylinder head, toward BDC. Both valves are closed.

Why this is the only stroke that makes power: the burning gas pushes on the piston, and the connecting rod turns that push into crankshaft rotation.
field3: On an upright drawing this is written as the piston moving down. In the Archer's flat engine the cylinders lie sideways, so think of it as toward or away from the cylinder head.

field1: Ramjet: how does it compress incoming air?
field2: It uses the aircraft's forward motion (ram air). There is no mechanical compressor.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P47 Jet ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2150 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Scramjet: what is it?
field2:
A ramjet variant that operates at hypersonic speeds with supersonic combustion inside the engine.

Hypersonic means faster than Mach 5. Example: NASA's X-43 test vehicle.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P44 Jet ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2090 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Turbofan: what does its large front fan do with most of the incoming air?
field2:
It diverts most of the air around the core (bypass air) to make thrust efficiently. That is why turbofans are highly efficient for modern airliners.

Why that saves fuel: pushing a lot of air a little faster takes less energy than pushing a little air a lot faster.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P43 Jet ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2070 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Turbojet: how does the air flow through it?
field2:
All the air passes through the core.

So all the thrust comes from the fast, hot jet out the back.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P43b Jet ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2080 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Turbojet: what kind of flight is it best for?
field2:
High-speed, high-altitude flight.

Why: a small, very fast exhaust jet works best when the airplane is flying fast too. At low speed much of its energy is wasted, so it burns a lot of fuel.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P45 Jet ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2110 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Turboshaft: what is it optimized to deliver?
field2:
Shaft power rather than jet thrust.

Example: in a helicopter the turbine turns a shaft geared to the rotor, and the exhaust gives almost no thrust.

Wide power range: the engine has to make full power for takeoff at sea level and still climb at altitude.

field2: Why each matters: long life between overhauls lowers cost; compact means a small cowling and less drag; easy access makes inspections quicker; low vibration protects the airframe, instruments and people.

field1: At what speed does the camshaft turn, relative to the crankshaft?
field2:
Always one-half crankshaft speed.

Why: each valve opens once per four-stroke cycle, and one cycle takes two crankshaft revolutions. The cam gear has twice as many teeth as the crankshaft gear.

field2: At lower altitudes and moderate speeds, with excellent low-speed performance. It is well suited to short runways and regional operations.

field2:
Why both valves are closed: the mixture has to be trapped so it can be squeezed. Squeezed mixture burns faster and pushes harder on the piston when it fires.

On an upright drawing this is written as the piston moving up. In the Archer's flat engine the cylinders lie sideways, so think of it as toward or away from the cylinder head.

tags: ConRod Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P80 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2660 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Connecting rod: what do the big-end bearing inserts do?
field2:
They reduce friction on the crankshaft journal.

The inserts are replaceable shells with a soft bearing surface. They ride on a thin film of pressurized oil, never metal on metal.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: ConRod Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P79 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2650 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Connecting rod: what does the big end do?
field2:
It houses the journal bearing that connects the rod to the crankshaft.

The big end goes around the crankpin, so it travels in a circle with the crankshaft while the small end only moves back and forth.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: ConRod Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P78 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2620 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Connecting rod: what does the rod beam (body) do?
field2:
It transmits the load between the piston and the crankshaft.

Why it is shaped like an I-beam: it carries thousands of pounds of push and pull on every stroke, yet it must stay light because it moves back and forth with the piston.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: ConRod Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P81 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2670 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Connecting rod: what does the rod cap do?
field2:
It secures the big-end assembly to the crankshaft.

The big end is split in two so it can be fitted around the crankpin. The cap is the removable half, and it is bolted on.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: ConRod Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P77 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2610 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Connecting rod: what does the small end do?
field2:
It connects the rod to the piston through the wrist pin.

The small end swings back and forth on the wrist pin as the crankshaft turns.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P35 Opposed ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_1960 Updated1005 Week2
field1:
Continental/Lycoming engine prefix codes:
{{c1::O}} = Opposed
{{c2::I}} = Fuel injected
{{c3::T}} = Turbocharged
{{c4::S}} = Supercharged
{{c5::G}} = Geared
{{c6::L}} = Left-hand rotation
field2: Example: the Archer's O-360 = Opposed, 360 cubic inches; no I (it has a carburetor) and no T (no turbocharger). A Cessna 172S's IO-360 is the same size but fuel-injected.

field1: Crankcase functions: {{c1::encloses and aligns the rotating crankshaft}}; {{c2::contains the main bearings that support the crankshaft journals}}; {{c3::seals in the oil to maintain lubrication and pressure}}.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P84 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2790 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what are the oil passages for?
field2:
They are internal channels that deliver pressurized lubrication (to the bearings).

Oil from the pump enters at the main journals and flows through holes drilled in the crankshaft out to the crankpins, so the connecting-rod bearings get oil too.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P82b ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2770 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what attaches to the crank pins?
field2:
The connecting rods.

The crankpins sit off the center line, so as the crankshaft turns they travel in a circle. That offset is what lets the rods turn the pistons' push into rotation.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P83b NewCard1005 PlaceAfter_W2_P83 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what do the counterweights do?
field2:
They balance the rotating crankshaft.

Why: the crankpins and rods are off center, so without weight on the opposite side the spinning crankshaft would shake the engine. The counterweights cut that vibration.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P83 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2780 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what do the crank webs (cheeks) do?
field2:
They connect the crankpins to the main journals.

They are the arms that hold each crankpin away from the center line, like the crank arm that holds a bicycle pedal.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P82 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2760 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what do the main journals do?
field2:
Support the rotating shaft. They ride in the main bearings.

The main journals are the smooth round sections on the crankshaft's center line. They spin inside the main bearings, which the crankcase holds, on a film of oil.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P85 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2800 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what does the flywheel mounting flange do?
field2:
It transfers the rotational power output to the drive system.

On an aircraft engine this is the propeller flange: the Archer's propeller bolts here.
field3: The name "flywheel mounting flange" comes from car crankshafts. Aircraft engines normally have no flywheel; the propeller does that job.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Crankshaft Final FLT328 ID_W2_P86 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2810 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Crankshaft: what does the keyway do?
field2:
It secures the timing gears and the accessory drive pulleys.

A keyway is a slot cut in the shaft. A small key fits in the slot and in the gear, so the gear can't slip around the shaft. That keeps the camshaft and magnetos timed to the crankshaft.

field1: Cylinder: what do the cooling fins do?
field2: Deep exterior fins increase the surface area for air cooling, maximizing heat dissipation. On aircraft cylinders they are cast into the aluminum-alloy head and machined into the steel barrel.

field1: Cylinder: what does the cylinder head house?
field2:
The intake and exhaust ports, the valve assembly, and the spark plug ports.

Why there: the head is where the mixture comes in, burns and goes out, so the valves that control the flow and the spark plugs that light it are mounted in it. Each cylinder has two spark plugs, one fired by each magneto.

tags: Core Cylinder Final FLT328 ID_W2_P68 ProfQ_W2_Q3 ProfQuestion ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Updated1003 Updated1005 Updated1006b Week2
field1: Cylinder: what does the mounting flange base do?
field2:
It is a heavy-duty base plate that anchors the cylinder assembly securely to the crankcase.

Why heavy-duty: every power stroke pushes the cylinder head outward, away from the crankcase, with thousands of pounds of force, and the flange carries that load.
field3: Studs screwed into the crankcase pass out through holes in the flange, and nuts tighten the flange down onto the crankcase. The flange is part of the steel barrel, at its base.

tags: Core Cylinder Final FLT328 ID_W2_P67 ProfQ_W2_Q3 ProfQuestion ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Updated1003 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Cylinder: what is the cylinder barrel?
field2:
The steel tube the piston slides in. Its hardened-steel interior bore gives the piston a smooth track to travel in.

Why hard and smooth: the piston rings rub against the bore on every stroke, so it must resist wear and give the rings a surface they can seal against.
field3: The bore is hardened by nitriding (heat-treating the steel's surface) or by chrome plating. Cooling fins are machined into the outside of the steel barrel (the aluminum head's fins are cast in). The head is screwed and shrunk onto the top of the barrel, and the mounting flange at the bottom bolts the cylinder to the crankcase.

field2: As potential (chemical) energy in the chemical bonds of the fuel.
field3: Examples of fuels: gasoline, jet fuel, hydrogen. Water is sometimes listed, but it is not a fuel: it is already-burned (oxidized) hydrogen and stores no usable chemical energy.

tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P25 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Reciprocating Seq_1860 Updated1005 Week2
field1: How are the cylinders arranged in a V-type engine?
field2:
In two in-line banks set at an angle to each other in a "V" shape, both driving a single shared crankshaft.

Example: the P-51 Mustang's V-12 has six cylinders in each bank.

field1: How are the cylinders arranged in a radial engine?
field2:
In a circle around a central crankshaft. The pistons radiate outward from a central hub in a star or ring pattern.

Each row has an odd number of cylinders (5, 7 or 9) so the firing order can skip every other cylinder and still space the power strokes evenly. Example: the Boeing Stearman.

field1: How is the camshaft driven?

field1: How many crankshaft revolutions does one complete four-stroke cycle take?
field2:
Two revolutions (720°), giving one power stroke per cylinder every two revolutions.

Why: each stroke is one half-turn (180°) of the crankshaft. Four strokes × 180° = 720° = 2 revolutions.

field1: In a V-type engine, what angle is typically set between the two cylinder banks?
field2:
Generally 60° apart.

Why 60°: most aircraft V engines were V-12s, like the P-51's Merlin. A four-stroke engine fires all its cylinders in two turns (720°), so a V-12 fires one every 60° (720° ÷ 12). Setting the banks 60° apart spaces the power strokes evenly.

The bank angle follows the cylinder count: a V-8 fires every 90° (720° ÷ 8), so V-8s use 90° banks.
field3: Some sources give a range of 30° to 60°. V-6 engines are often built at 60° or 90° with offset crankpins on the crankshaft to even out the firing.

field1: In a heat engine, at what point in the cycle is the heat of combustion released?
field2:
At a point in the cycle where the pressure is high.

Why: heat added to gas that is already squeezed tight gives the biggest push. In a piston engine the spark fires near top dead center, at the end of the compression stroke.

field1: Math: a rocker arm's valve side is 1.5 times as long as its push-rod side. The push rod rises 0.3 inch. How far does the valve open?

Valve lift = push-rod lift × lever ratio

field1: Piston: what do the compression rings do?
field2:
They seal in the combustion gases.

Why rings are needed: the piston must be slightly smaller than the bore so it can slide and grow when hot. The rings spring outward against the bore and close that gap, so the gas pushes the piston instead of leaking past it.

field2:
They support the ring grooves.

The lands are the bands of piston metal between the grooves. Each land holds a ring in its own groove so it can't twist or shift along the piston.

field1: Piston: what does the oil control ring do?
field2:
It regulates the thickness of the oil film on the cylinder wall.

Why: the rings need a thin oil film to slide without wearing, but oil left on the wall above the piston gets burned. The oil control ring scrapes off the extra and sends it back through the oil drain holes to the crankcase.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P74 Piston ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2440 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Piston: what does the skirt do?
field2:
It guides the piston's alignment in the bore.

The skirt is the lower part of the piston, below the rings. It keeps the piston from rocking (tilting) in the bore as the connecting rod pushes on it at an angle.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P71 Piston ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2410 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Piston: what is the crown (head)?
field2:
The top surface. It receives the expansion forces from combustion and forms the lower boundary of the combustion chamber.

Why it matters: the crown takes the full heat and push of combustion, so it is the hottest part of the piston. Damage from detonation or pre-ignition (a cracked, melted or holed crown) shows up here first.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P75 Piston ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2460 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Piston: what is the wrist pin boss?
field2:
The reinforced internal structure that anchors the wrist pin connection to the connecting rod.

The wrist pin passes through the two bosses and through the small end of the connecting rod, so the rod can swing while the piston slides straight. The bosses are thick because the whole combustion force passes through them into the pin.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core EngineTypes Final FLT328 ID_W2_P15 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_1770 Updated1005 Week2
field1: Pulse-jet and rocket: how is compression achieved?
field2:
Through combustion itself.

In a pulse-jet, each burst of combustion builds pressure in the chamber; then valves at the front reopen to let in the next charge. Example: the World War II V-1 "buzz bomb".

field1: Ramjet: how is compression achieved?
field2:
Ram compression, from the engine's high forward speed. There is no mechanical compressor.

Why it can't start on its own: with no forward speed there is no compression, so a ramjet must first be boosted to high speed.

field1: Reciprocating aircraft engines are categorized primarily by what?
field2:
Their cylinder arrangement.

The four arrangements are in-line, opposed, V-type and radial. Arrangement decides how wide the engine is (drag), how well the cylinders cool, and how much power fits in the cowling.

field1: Reciprocating engine: how is compression achieved?
field2:
By the reciprocating (back-and-forth) action of the pistons.

Example: on the compression stroke, the Archer's pistons squeeze the fuel/air mixture into the small space at the cylinder head.
field3: Working fluid: fuel/air mixture. Propulsive fluid: ambient air.

field1: Rocker arm: how is valve clearance maintained?
field2:
With an adjusting screw or a hydraulic lash adjuster.

Why clearance is needed: metal parts grow as they heat up. A small gap lets the valve still close fully when the engine is hot.
The Archer's Lycoming uses hydraulic lash adjusters (hydraulic tappets), so pilots and mechanics don't set it by hand.

field1: Rocker arm: how is it lubricated?
field2:
By continuous oil flow through internal passages, which minimizes pivot wear.

In Lycoming engines the oil reaches the rocker through the hollow push rod, then drains back down to the sump.

field1: The four strokes of a 4-stroke internal combustion cylinder, in order: {{c1::intake}}, {{c2::compression}}, {{c3::power}}, {{c4::exhaust}}.
field2:
The power stroke is sometimes called the combustion stroke.

Why four: the piston needs one stroke each to pull in the mixture, squeeze it, be pushed by the burning gas, and push the burned gas out. Only the power stroke drives the crankshaft; the other three are paid for by the momentum of the crankshaft and the other cylinders' power strokes.

At high altitude and high speed. That is why turbine airliners typically cruise in the flight levels.

Why: in the thin, cold air up high the airplane has less drag, and the engine runs more efficiently.

field2: They let the oil scraped off the cylinder wall by the oil control ring drain back through the piston to the crankcase.

field2: It meters fuel into the incoming air to make the fuel/air mixture.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides

field2: It sprays metered fuel into each cylinder's intake port (or into the cylinder) instead of mixing it in a carburetor.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 HeatEngine ID_W2_P01 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_1590 Updated1005 Week2
field1: What does a heat engine do?
field2:
It converts the chemical energy of fuel into heat energy, then into mechanical energy, by the flow of some fluid mass through the engine.

Example: in the Archer, gasoline (chemical energy) burns in the cylinders (heat), and the hot gas pushes the pistons (mechanical). The fluid mass is the air drawn through the engine.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P95 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Seq_2970 Updated1005 Updated1006 ValveTrain Week2
field1: What does a rocker arm do?
field2:
It pivots on a shaft (fulcrum) so that when the push rod pushes one end, the other end pushes the valve stem into the cylinder head and opens the valve. When the push rod eases off, the valve spring closes the valve.

It works like a seesaw: push one end and the other end moves the opposite way.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Definition FLT328 Glossary ID_W2_G22 Quiz1 Seq_1940 Week2
field1: What does a supercharger do?
field2: It compresses the intake air, forcing more air into the cylinders than the outside air pressure alone would push in.
field3: A supercharger is usually driven by the engine itself (gears or belt).

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides

field1: What does a valve split key (keeper) do?
field2: Its two tapered halves lock the valve spring retainer onto the valve stem.

field1: What does an engine's accessory gearbox do?
field2: It drives the engine's accessories, such as the fuel and oil pumps, the generator, and the starter.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides

field1: What does the connecting rod connect?
field2:
The piston to the crankshaft.

Picture a bicycle: your knee moves back and forth like the piston, your shin is the connecting rod, and the pedal crank goes around like the crankshaft.
field3: Together with the crankshaft, it converts the piston's reciprocating motion into rotary motion.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides

field1: What does the exhaust valve do?
field2:
It lets the burned exhaust gases escape the cylinder after combustion.

It opens near the end of the power stroke and stays open while the piston pushes the burned gas out. It runs much hotter than the intake valve because exhaust gas over 1,000 °F flows past it.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides

field1: What does the intake valve control?
field2:
The flow of fuel/air mixture into the combustion chamber.

It opens for the intake stroke, when the piston moves away from the head and draws the mixture in.

tags: Core Elaboration Final FLT328 ID_W2_P96b NewCard1005 PlaceAfter_W2_P96 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Scenario Updated1005 ValveTrain Week2
field1: What happens if a valve has too little clearance?
field2: When the engine heats up and the parts grow, the valve can't close fully. Hot gas leaks past it, the cylinder loses compression, and an exhaust valve can burn.
field3: Too much clearance does the opposite: the valve opens late, closes early, doesn't open as far, and the valve train is noisy.

field1: What happens to the crankshaft bearings if oil pressure is lost?
field2: The oil film that holds each bearing off the crankshaft disappears. Metal rubs on metal, the bearing overheats and can seize, and a connecting rod can break.
field3: That is why oil pressure is checked right after start, and why low oil pressure in flight calls for landing as soon as possible.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Elaboration Final FLT328 ID_W2_P73b NewCard1005 Piston PlaceAfter_W2_P73 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Scenario Updated1005 Week2
field1: What happens when a piston's oil control ring is worn?
field2: Too much oil stays on the cylinder wall and gets burned in the combustion chamber. Oil consumption goes up, and the oil fouls the spark plugs and builds carbon deposits.
field3: Fouled plugs can show up as a rough engine or a larger-than-normal RPM drop on the mag check.

deck: FLT 328-A Aircraft Systems::Quiz 1 · Wk 1–2::Wk 02 · Quiz 1 · Engine Types & Construction — Professor Slides
tags: Core Elaboration Final FLT328 ID_W2_P72b NewCard1005 Piston PlaceAfter_W2_P72 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Scenario Updated1005 Week2
field1: What happens when an engine's compression rings are worn?
field2: Combustion gas leaks past the rings into the crankcase. This is called blow-by. The cylinder loses compression and power, and a compression check shows a low reading for that cylinder.
field3: Blow-by also pushes oil mist out the crankcase breather and dirties the oil faster.

tags: Core Final FLT328 ID_W2_P18 ProfSlides Quiz1 QuizSep29 Reciprocating Seq_1810 Updated1005 Week2
field1: What is a reciprocating engine?
field2:
An internal combustion engine, common in general aviation, that converts fuel energy into mechanical power by moving pistons inside cylinders, which then turn a propeller.

"Reciprocating" means moving back and forth: the pistons go back and forth, and the crankshaft turns that motion into rotation.
Example: the Archer's Lycoming O-360 and the Cessna 172's Lycoming O-320 are both reciprocating engines.

field1: What is a turbocharger?
field2: A supercharger whose compressor is driven by a turbine spun by the engine's exhaust gas.
field3: Exhaust spins the turbine; the turbine and compressor share one shaft, so the compressor spins too and packs extra air into the cylinders. A gear- or belt-driven supercharger (W2_G22) takes power from the crankshaft; a turbocharger uses exhaust energy that would otherwise go overboard.

field2:

field1: What is the main function of a piston?
field2:
To receive the force of the expanding combustion gases and transmit it, through the connecting rod, to the crankshaft.

Example: at 500 psi of gas pressure, the Archer's 5⅛-inch piston (about 20 square inches) is pushed with about 10,000 lb of force on each power stroke.
field3:
Its back-and-forth strokes also draw in, compress, and push out the gases during the four-stroke cycle.

field1: What is the job of the engine valves?
field2:
To let air (the fuel/air mixture) into the cylinders and let exhaust out.

Each cylinder has one intake and one exhaust valve. They open and close at exact points in the four-stroke cycle and must seal tightly the rest of the time, or the cylinder loses compression and power.

field1: Why is a radial engine's propeller turned through by hand before starting?
field2: To check for hydraulic lock. While the engine sits, oil drains into the lower cylinders. A piston can't squeeze liquid, so starting with a cylinder full of oil can bend or break a connecting rod. Turning the propeller by hand shows a locked cylinder before the starter is used.
field3: Opposed engines like the Archer's avoid this because the cylinders lie flat, so oil drains back to the sump instead of pooling in a cylinder.

field1:
Dynamic damper
A {{c1::pendulum}} mounted in the crankshaft's {{c2::counterweight}} assembly, free to swing in a small arc → it is tuned to the frequency of the engine's {{c3::power impulses}} → when that vibration occurs, the pendulum swings {{c4::out of time with the crankshaft vibration}} → vibration is {{c5::reduced to a minimum}}.
field2: Built as a slotted steel counterweight on the crankcheek, held by spool-shaped pins in oversized holes, which gives the pendulum effect.

field1:
Hydraulic lifter cycle
Valve closed, follower on the cam's base circle → the {{c1::plunger spring}} pushes the plunger out, removing clearance → the {{c2::ball check valve}} opens and oil fills the {{c3::pressure chamber}} → the cam lifts the tappet, seating the check valve → the trapped oil acts as a {{c4::cushion (solid link)}} to open the valve → a {{c5::predetermined leakage}} compensates for expansion → after the valve closes, the chamber refills.

Hollow stem partly filled with metallic {{c1::sodium}} → it melts at about {{c2::208 °F}} → valve motion sloshes it, carrying heat from the {{c3::valve head to the stem}} → heat leaves through the valve guide to the head and fins → valve temperature drops {{c4::300–400 °F}}.

Why there is a firing order: the cylinders fire in a spread-out pattern, not front to back, so the pushes on the crankshaft alternate side to side and front to back. That keeps the engine balanced and the power strokes evenly spaced.

In opposed engines, cylinders usually fire in pairs across the center main bearing.

field1: What is an engine's firing order?
field2:
The sequence in which the power events occur in the different cylinders.

Example: the Lycoming O-320 in a Cessna 172 fires 1-3-2-4. Cylinders are numbered from the front, with 1 at the right front, so the sparks go right front, right rear, left front, left rear.
field3: One cylinder fires every 180° of crank rotation, so all four fire once in two turns (720°). Continental numbers its cylinders from the rear, so the same numbers mean different positions on a Continental.

field1: A naturally aspirated (unsupercharged) engine's volumetric efficiency is typically {{c1::less than 100%}}.
field2:
Only forced induction (a supercharger) can push it above 100%.

Why under 100%: the air loses pressure flowing through the air filter, carburetor and intake pipes, and it heats up on the way in, so less fills the cylinder. The Archer's engine is normally aspirated.

field1: An opposed four-cylinder engine has a 4-inch bore (piston diameter) and a 5-inch stroke. Using π ≈ 3, what is its total displacement?
field2:
240 cubic inches

r = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 in
A = π × r² ≈ 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 sq in
One cylinder: V = A × H = 12 × 5 = 60 cu in
Four cylinders: 60 × 4 = 240 cu in
field3: With π = 3.14 the answer is about 251 cubic inches. The Lycoming O-320 in a Cessna 172 works the same way: about 80 cubic inches per cylinder × 4 = 320 cubic inches, which is where the 320 in its name comes from.

field1: Detonation causes: {{c1::excessive heat}}; {{c2::excessive pressure}}; {{c3::poor fuel quality or low octane}}; {{c4::a lean fuel/air mixture}}.
field2:
Why each one causes it: heat and pressure push the unburned mixture past the point where it lights by itself. Low-octane fuel resists that less. A lean mixture at high power burns hotter.

That is why the Archer must use at least the fuel grade in its POH (it normally burns 100LL avgas).

field1: During a mag check, what does it mean that a magneto is grounded?
field2:
Its circuit is connected to ground, so it cannot make sparks. The engine runs on the other magneto.

The magneto switch does the grounding: it connects that magneto's P-lead to ground.
field3: The P-lead is the wire from each magneto's primary circuit to the magneto switch. Ground on an airplane is the metal of the airframe and engine, not the earth.

field1: During a mag check, what happens when the magneto switch is turned to L (left)?
field2:
Only the left magneto operates; the right magneto is grounded (turned off).

"L" names the magneto that stays running, not a side of the engine.

Why pilots do it: in the run-up, each magneto alone should give a small RPM drop. No drop, a big drop, or rough running points to a magneto, plug or lead problem. The Archer's POH allows up to 175 RPM drop on either magneto, with no more than 50 RPM difference between them.

field2:

field1: In a multi-cylinder four-stroke engine, how do the cylinders' cycles line up?
field2:
They are staggered: each cylinder is at a different stage of the cycle on each stroke.

Example: in the Archer's four-cylinder O-360, at any moment one cylinder is on intake, one on compression, one on power and one on exhaust. Each crankshaft half-turn, a different cylinder fires (1-3-2-4), so the engine gets a power stroke every 180°.
field3:
That is why the cylinders take turns firing (firing order) to balance the engine. In the animation, watch the opposite cylinders #1 and #2: their pistons reach the head together, but one is starting power while the other starts intake.

field1: In detonation, what part of the charge explodes?
field2:
The end gas: after the spark plug fires, the remaining mixture explodes instead of burning smoothly.

Why the end gas: the flame front spreading from the spark plug squeezes and heats the unburned mixture ahead of it. If that end gas gets too hot, it lights all at once instead of waiting for the flame.

field1: Lycoming (cross-wired): the LEFT magneto fires the {{c1::top plugs on even}} cylinders and the {{c2::bottom plugs on odd}} cylinders.
field2:
The RIGHT magneto is the reverse: bottom plugs on even cylinders, top plugs on odd cylinders.

One reason for cross-wiring: bottom plugs foul more easily, because oil and lead deposits collect low in the cylinder. Cross-wiring gives each magneto some top plugs, so neither one has only the plugs most likely to foul.
The Archer's O-360 is a Lycoming, so it is cross-wired.

field1: Math: the crankpin sits 2.2 inches from the crankshaft's center line (the crank throw). How long is the piston's stroke?
field2:
4.4 inches

Stroke = 2 × crank throw
2 × 2.2 in = 4.4 in

The crankpin swings 2.2 in toward the cylinder at TDC and 2.2 in away at BDC, so the piston travels twice the throw.
field3:
The Archer's O-360 has a 4.375-inch stroke (crank throw about 2.19 in).

field1: On an airplane, what is electrical ground?
field2:
The metal structure of the airframe and engine, which every circuit uses as its return path.

It has nothing to do with the earth: a flying airplane carries its own ground with it.
field3: The engine sits on rubber mounts, so ground straps connect it to the airframe. Each magneto case is bolted to the engine, so it is grounded through the engine. A spark plug's ground electrode returns the spark current through the cylinder head the same way.

field1: What is pre-ignition and detonation, and how do you resolve it?
field2:
Pre-ignition: the charge ignites before the spark, from a hot spot (hot carbon, hot spark plug, overheated parts), made more likely by high cylinder pressure.
Detonation: after the spark, the end gas explodes instead of burning smoothly (excessive heat and pressure, low-octane fuel, lean mixture).
Resolve: reduce power, enrich the mixture, increase cooling (and use the proper fuel); for pre-ignition reduce power immediately and land as soon as practical if it persists.

field1: What is pre-ignition?
field2:
Ignition of the fuel/air charge before the spark plug fires, while the piston is still compressing the charge.

Why it is so harmful: the mixture starts burning while the piston is still moving toward the cylinder head, so the rising pressure pushes against the piston instead of with it. The heat builds up fast.

Example of a hot spot: a glowing carbon deposit or an overheated spark plug tip.

The point where the piston is nearest the cylinder head.

field1: When dragging an object horizontally, what does the force required depend on?
field2:
Friction between the object and the ground. Friction depends on:
1. how rough both surfaces are (the object's bottom and the ground)
2. how hard the object presses down: its weight, which comes from its mass

Contact area makes almost no difference.
field3: Getting the object moving takes a bit more force than keeping it moving. Work can be done in any direction: lifting vertically or dragging horizontally.

field1: Who set the value of one horsepower, and from what?
field2:
James Watt, from the rate at which an English workhorse could work.

Why a horse: Watt sold steam engines to mine owners who used horses to pump water and haul loads. Rating his engines in horsepower told buyers how many horses an engine could replace.

field1: Why do you do a mag check before takeoff?
field2: To prove that each magneto, with its leads and plugs, can run the engine by itself. Dual ignition is only a backup if both halves work.
field3: What the RPM tells you: a small drop is normal, because one plug per cylinder burns the mixture more slowly. A big drop or rough running points to a fouled plug, a bad lead or a bad magneto. No drop at all means the switch isn't grounding the other magneto, so that magneto stays hot even at OFF.

field1: Valve lead = a valve opening {{c1::before}} TDC or BDC (e.g., the intake valve opening before TDC). Valve lag = a valve closing {{c2::after}} TDC or BDC (e.g., the exhaust valve closing after TDC, or the intake valve closing after BDC).

field1: All else equal, how does piston displacement affect horsepower?
field2:
The greater the displacement, the greater the maximum horsepower the engine can develop.

Why: a bigger displacement pulls in more fuel/air mixture on each intake stroke, so each power stroke burns more fuel and releases more energy.

Example: the Cessna 172's O-320 makes 150–160 hp; the Archer's O-360, with about 40 cu in more displacement, makes 180 hp.

The volume the piston displaces moving from BDC to TDC (cubic inches in most American engines).

Example: the Archer's O-360 has a 5.125-inch bore (about 20.6 sq in of piston area) and a 4.375-inch stroke. One cylinder displaces 20.6 × 4.375 ≈ 90 cu in, and four cylinders ≈ 361 cu in. That is where the 360 in its name comes from.

field1: What is thermal efficiency?
field2:

Example: at 25–30%, only about a quarter of the fuel's heat turns into useful work; the rest leaves as heat.

field1: What is the compression ratio?
field2:
Cylinder volume with the piston at BDC compared with the volume with the piston at TDC.

Why it matters: the more the mixture is squeezed before it burns, the harder it pushes on the piston, so a higher compression ratio gives more power from the same fuel. Too high, and the mixture can detonate, so higher compression needs higher-octane fuel.

Example: the Archer's O-360 has a compression ratio of 8.5:1.

field1: What is the stroke?
field2:
The distance the piston moves from one end of the cylinder to the other: from top dead center (TDC) to bottom dead center (BDC), or back.

Example: the Archer's O-360 has a 4.375-inch stroke. In its flat cylinders the piston travels sideways, between the point nearest the cylinder head (TDC) and the point farthest from it (BDC).

field1: What is the risk of opening the intake valve too early?
field2:
Hot gases left from the previous cycle can flash back into the intake manifold and ignite the mixture there: a backfire.

Why: near TDC the cylinder still holds hot, burning exhaust gas. If the intake valve opens too soon, that gas meets the fresh mixture in the intake manifold and lights it there instead of in the cylinder.

field1: When does the exhaust valve open?
field2:
Considerably before BDC on the power stroke: about 50° to 75° before BDC on some engines.

Why so early: by 50–75° before BDC the piston has already got most of the push it can get. Opening the exhaust valve then lets the remaining pressure start blowing the gas out, so the piston doesn't have to push against it on the exhaust stroke.

field1: When does the intake valve close?
field2:
About 50° to 75° past bottom dead center on the compression stroke (depending on the engine).

Why so late: the incoming mixture has momentum and keeps flowing in after BDC. Closing late packs more mixture into the cylinder, so the engine makes more power.

field2:
About 8° to 55° before TDC on the exhaust stroke (varies by engine).

Why so early: the exhaust is still rushing out and leaves low pressure behind it, so opening the intake valve before TDC lets that flow start pulling in the fresh charge. The exact number depends on the engine, which is why the range is so wide.

field1: Why does the intake valve open well before TDC on the exhaust stroke?
field2:
To induce a greater charge of fuel/air into the cylinder, increasing horsepower.

How it works: near the end of the exhaust stroke, the fast-moving exhaust leaves a low pressure in the cylinder. An intake valve that is already open lets fresh mixture rush in on that low pressure, so more mixture gets in before the intake stroke even starts.

field2:
As the gases expand and the chamber volume grows during the power stroke, the temperature drops.

Example: by the time the gas leaves the exhaust valve, a light piston engine's exhaust gas temperature is typically about 1,200–1,600 °F, far below the 3,000–4,000 °F peak.

No propeller is 100% efficient (if it were, THP would equal BHP); its efficiency varies with engine speed, attitude, altitude, temperature, and airspeed.

Example: the Archer has a fixed-pitch propeller, so its blade angle is a compromise. It is most efficient at one combination of RPM and airspeed and less efficient in climb or at high speed.

field1: Why is the spark timed before top dead center?
field2:
Burning takes time; firing early ensures combustion is complete by the time the piston is slightly past TDC.

What goes wrong otherwise: fire at TDC and the pressure peaks late, after the piston is already moving away from the head, so power is wasted. Fire too early and the pressure rises while the piston is still moving toward the head, fighting the engine and overheating it.

Leftover exhaust dilutes the fresh fuel/air charge at the start of the next cycle.

field1: How does an air-cooled aircraft engine remove and control excess heat?
field2:
Remove the heat: the cowling takes in air, the baffles force it over the cylinder cooling fins, and the heated air leaves through the cowl exit at the bottom rear.
Control the airflow (two different devices; an airplane usually has one or the other):
• Cowl flaps: doors the pilot opens to make the exit bigger (more cooling, more drag).
• Augmenter tubes: the exhaust jet sucks hot air out of the cowling (automatic, no pilot action).
Oil: carries heat from inside the engine to the oil cooler.
Monitor: the CHT (cylinder head temperature) gauge shows how hot the cylinders are.

field1: What is a thermocouple?
field2: Two different metals joined at a junction. A temperature difference between that junction and the instrument end makes a small voltage, which the gauge reads as temperature.
field3:
In the CHT system the hot end sits in the cylinder head (threaded in, or as the spark-plug gasket) and the cold end is at the cockpit gauge. The bigger the temperature difference, the higher the voltage, so the gauge needs no battery to sense it.

The second picture shows the real parts: the probe in the cylinder head, the shielded leads through the firewall, the electrical connector and the CHT gauge. field1: What is thermal shock, what conditions can cause it, and how can a pilot help prevent it?
field2:
What: rapid cooling of a hot engine; metals contract unevenly → cylinder-head cracking.
Causes: sudden power reductions, e.g., power-off maneuvers right after a climb, chopping power for descent, high-speed idle descents.
Prevent: cool the engine after a climb before power-off maneuvers; reduce power gradually, well before descent; close cowl flaps; avoid high airspeed at idle.

field1: Why does an aircraft engine need a turbocharger to keep its power as it climbs?
field2: Air gets thinner with altitude, so each intake stroke draws in less air and the engine makes less power. The turbocharger packs extra air into the cylinders, so the engine keeps its power higher up.
field3: How: exhaust spins the turbine, the shared shaft spins the compressor, and the compressor pushes the packed air to the cylinders. The waste gate (W4_G01) controls how much it packs in.

field1: Why is a propeller blade twisted, with a lower blade angle near the tip than near the hub?
field2: The tip travels farther around each turn, so it moves faster and its relative wind comes in flatter. A lower blade angle there keeps the angle of attack about the same along the whole blade, so every part of the blade does useful work.
field3:
This also spreads the thrust load evenly along the blade instead of piling it on the fast-moving tip, which keeps stress at the tip down. The twist gives every part of the blade the same forward distance per turn, which is why a prop's pitch is quoted at one point (usually 75% of the radius).

field3: As the airplane climbs and the air thins, the controller closes the gate a little at a time to keep manifold pressure up. Engine oil pressure moves it.

field1: On a conventional twin, why is the left engine the critical engine?
field2: At high angle of attack (low speed, high power), each propeller's thrust is centered on its descending blade, on the right side of its disk. field1: Where is a propeller's blade angle lowest, and why?
field2: Near the tip: the tip travels fastest, so its relative wind is flattest; twisting the blade (low angle at the tip, high at the shank) keeps angle of attack about the same along the blade.
field3: Built that way on purpose; also keeps tip loads and stresses down.

field2:
Idle: supplies fuel below about 1,000 RPM, when venturi airflow is too weak, using the low pressure at the nearly closed throttle.
Acceleration: adds extra fuel when the throttle opens quickly, preventing a lean flat spot.
Power enrichment (economizer): adds fuel at full throttle so it absorbs heat and cools the engine; lean and economical otherwise.
Carburetor heat: sends exhaust-heated air to the carburetor to prevent or melt carburetor ice (use full heat, early).

field1: What is the difference between complete and incomplete combustion, and what are their byproducts?
field2:
Complete: enough oxygen to burn all the fuel: 2 C₈H₁₈ + 25 O₂ → 16 CO₂ + 18 H₂O + heat (the most heat).
Incomplete: not enough oxygen: carbon monoxide (CO) forms instead of CO₂ (2 C₈H₁₈ + 17 O₂ → 16 CO + 18 H₂O + heat), and with even less oxygen free carbon (black smoke, soot); less heat is released.
Other exhaust byproducts: small amounts of unburned oil and soot, lead oxides from leaded fuel, and oxides of other additives. Excess air leaves unused oxygen.

field1: What types of fuel contamination can occur, and how can they affect aircraft safety?
field2:
Solids (dust, dirt, bugs, lint): plug screens, the gascolator and injectors.
Surfactants: carry other contaminants down as sludge.
Water: condenses as fuel cools, sinks to the sumps, freezes and clogs screens.
Soluble fuels such as jet fuel: mix in invisibly (mis-fueling, detonation).
Result: restricted fuel flow, power loss, fuel starvation and engine failure.
